speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATION TO BE CONSIDERED
speechtext:
The right hon. leader of the government wishes to make a short announcement.
In accord with the understanding reached at the party leaders' meeting this morning I wish to announce merely that after three separate discussions and in spite of our best efforts, we were unable to agree on a program or timetable of work for the rest of the session.
Speaking on behalf of the government I should inform the house, as I promised to do, that the government considers the following matters should be dealt with before Christmas, and I give them not necessarily in order of time priority. First, estimates; redistribution bill; report of the flag committee; the labour standards bill and the pensions bill.
The order of business proposed for this week has already, I think, been given to the house. Today, as the house knows, we will be dealing with the pensions resolution, and tomorrow and the rest of the week-on Wednesday the house will not be sitting- redistribution and estimates. It should be possible, I believe, to deal with the matters I have mentioned in a month or so. If we do better than that and there is additional time before Christmas, there are other measures on the order paper which could be brought forward. I also have to make the customary and necessary reservation that any program of work is always subject to change due to any emergency developing.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATION TO BE CONSIDERED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party regret that we have not been able to work out a satisfactory timetable for the business of the house for the balance of this session. However, I should like to stress two things which as far as this party is concerned are well known. We are desirous of accomplishing two things, and I place them in their order of importance.


First of all, we are desirous that a limited legislative program be completed before the end of this session. We would place as the essential items in that program the Canada pension plan, the labour standards act, the redistribution bill and the estimates. We think those matters ought to have top priority.
Second, we are interested in having the report of the flag committee disposed of. Indications are that there is very wide support in this house for that report, including support from members of all political parties in the house. I am told that at one time on a vote all 14 members of the committee voted in favour of a single maple leaf flag. However, it is not my intention to discuss the flag question at the moment but simply to say that we are quite anxious to see the flag question disposed of. But we are not prepared to pay as the price for disposing of the flag question the sidetracking of any of the legislative items which I have mentioned.
For that reason I do hope that the items which the Prime Minister read out are not necessarily to be taken in the order in which he read them. We would hope that redistribution, the labour code and the Canada pension plan can be disposed of before we deal with the report of the committee on the flag. I see no reason why we cannot dispose of all the items, including the flag question, but I do make a special appeal to the government not to allow the debate on the flag committee report to prevent us passing the other more vital and important items. I also hope that when the flag question comes up, even though we have not been able to agree on a limitation of time we will have the co-operation of the official opposition in disposing of it with the greatest possible dispatch.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATION TO BE CONSIDERED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if every party in this house had shown good faith in determining the legislative program to be passed before the end of the session, we could have reached an understanding and settled the problems which face us at this moment.
After attending a meeting, I believe that it was especially good faith which was lacking on the part of the official opposition. Only a few items remain to be discussed before the end of the session. This year we have already beaten the record for the length of any session. We discussed the flag issue for more than 22 days, and it still seems to be the stumbling block. In my opinion, this is a

lesson for the Canadian people, because if the 265 members in this house cannot come to an agreement, how can we expect any agreement in Canada on the most important problems?
Mr. Speaker, I say that bad faith in some quarters prevented us from coming to an agreement and that will happen again in this house as well as throughout the country.
For instance, again today at noon following the very sensible statement made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) challenged the government with regard to the imposition of closure. Such a stand is an obvious proof of bad faith because the government has not talked about closure yet.
When the leader of the official opposition states that 30 members of his party want to talk on that matter, that means of course 15 hours of debate or roughly three sitting days.
I feel that things should be settled once and for all because the four other parties were ready to agree to the suggestion that the bills dealing with the pension plan and redistribution as well as the labour code be adopted first. If it had been possible to come to an agreement on the consideration of the estimates, we could have ended this session and passed all the items which have yet to be considered.
I believe that it would have been very easy to come to an agreement, and if we did not reach one I think that all those party leaders' meetings should stop as long as good faith is not the basis for discussion between the leaders of the political parties in this house.

subtopic: MR. MACEWAN-DISCLOSURES TO PRESS RESPECTING NEW INDUSTRIES
MR. MACEWAN-DISCLOSURES TO PRESS RESPECTING NEW INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a short question of privilege which affects all members of the house and particularly the people of the province of Nova Scotia and the constituency I represent. It has reference to a press report in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of last Saturday, November 7, dealing with a statement by Premier Robert Stanfield. The report reads in part as follows:
Premier Robert Stanfield yesterday scored what he termed "federal authorities" and "federal sources" for premature disclosure to the press of secret negotiations that have been going on concerning three industries interested in settling in the province.
Reference is made to a proposed car plant for the Sydney area of Cape Breton, a

Question of Privilege
recording machine manufacturing company for Halifax, namely the Clairtone company, and a pulp and paper mill for Pictou county. The premier went on to point out that negotiations had been going on between the provincial government and these companies, and that disclosures had been made to the press by what he referred to as federal authorities and federal sources in Ottawa. The article goes on to report him as saying:
"Yesterday when I read the federal disclosure regarding Clairtone I understood for the first time the depth of Angus L. Macdonald's exasperation with Ottawa."
I hope it will not be repeated. My question of privilege is that when questions were asked of certain ministers during debate in the house with regard to industries which had signified their intention to settle in designated areas, those questions were not answered because we were told it might prejudice the negotiations. Apparently these ministers have now seen fit to allow some of their officials, referred to by the premier as "federal authorities" and "federal sources", to disclose this information, thereby making it possible that the negotiations will break down and these industries will be lost to the province of Nova Scotia.
I therefore submit to the Prime Minister that this practice should be stopped, that it should not take place again in the future, and that these federal officials and sources should wait until negotiations are fully completed and the province is assured of these industries. I point out particularly that it has been stated that the Scott Paper Company proposes to settle in the county I represent, a county of high unemployment for many years. This is an excellent opportunity, and I hope that industry will not be lost to the good people of that historic county.

speechtext:
1.	Have surveys been made, by employees of the federal government or by Independent oceanographers, in the strait of Belle Isle, with a view to studying the possibility of constructing a causeway nine miles long in a body of water 150 feet deep between Labrador and Newfoundland?
2.	If so, what were the conclusions of such surveys with respect to preventing cold water currents from penetrating into the gulf of St. Lawrence and adversely affecting the weather in the marl-times and the province of Quebec?
3.	If no surveys have yet been undertaken will consideration be given to ascertaining the pros and cons of a project which could be undertaken by the federal government to connect Newfoundland to the continent through the extension of the trans-Canada highway, the construction of a railway line by the C.N.R. and the installation of electric transmission cables?

subtopic: STUDY OF CAUSEWAY, LABRADOR-NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
1. No survey has been conducted for this specific purpose; however, surveys have been made by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to assess seasonal temperature and salinity conditions, to forecast ice freeze-up and breakup, and to study the movement of water through the strait.
2.	The results of these studies to this date indicate that the flow of water through Belle Isle strait varies in direction and speed across the strait, and fluctuates in time in response to meteorological changes. These variations in time and space are such that there is no clear evidence that on the average there is any substantial cooling of the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence because of the net flow through Belle Isle strait.
3.	A survey of this magnitude would require decisions by the government as a whole.

speechtext:
The hon. member's question probably stems from a report in one of the Toronto daily papers. I may say that I had a discussion of a general nature in the course of a meeting which took place between the attorney general of Quebec and myself last Thursday on the occasion of an address which I delivered in Montreal. It is more than probable that the words in the statement which may have been made subsequently by the attorney general of Quebec in relation to the administration of the parole system have been misreported, because I am completely conscious and aware, and I am sure Mr. Wagner is also aware, that under the National Parole Act neither the commission nor the government may undertake to submit the decisions of the national parole boards to the approval or the veto of any outside authority.
Furthermore, I am aware that the question as to who ought to be consulted by the national parole board and when such consultation ought to take place is one of internal policy for the chairman and the members of the national parole board themselves. If, for instance, the parole board were of the opinion that it would be advisable to obtain the views of the attorney general of a province in a case where the public safety is involved, that practice would be up to the parole board itself to adopt, and not up to the government.
Anyhow, I could not have made any such undertaking as has been reported, because before our discussions Mr. Wagner and myself had told newspapermen that we would probably not be in a position to make a joint statement to them after our meeting because in that most informal meeting we were not permitted, and it would not have been appropriate for us, to bind our respective governments.

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure, to be known as the Canada pension plan, to establish in Canada a comprehensive program of retirement pensions payable to contributors; to provide for the payment of supplementary benefits, including benefits for the widows and orphans of contributors and benefits to contributors who become disabled; to provide for the co-ordination of pensions payable under the Old Age Security Act with benefits payable under the Canada pension plan and for the payment of adjusted pensions under the Old Age Security Act beginning at any age from 65 years; to provide for the adjustment of pensions and other benefits in line with increases in earnings and the cost of living; to provide that funds arising from the operation of the Canada pension plan shall be invested in securities of the provinces, provincially guaranteed securities of provincial crown agents, and securities of Canada; and to provide further that all expenditures under the Canada pension plan, including costs of administration, shall be financed from contributions by employees and employers and from contributions by persons in respect of self-employed earnings.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is perhaps unfortunate that in dealing with this matter today the committee will only have a total of some four hours. However, since we are proceeding under the new rules and hon. members are restricted to 20 minute speeches, it is hoped that a great many members will be able to participate.
Earlier this year, Mr. Chairman, we had an opportunity to discuss a resolution similar to that now before the committee which preceded Bill No. C-75. However, the resolution which is before the committee today goes much further than the earlier version and introduces a social insurance measure of much wider scope. This more comprehensive program has been made possible by a number
tMr. Diefenbaker.]
of developments, many of which hon. members are aware of, which have taken place in the past several months.
It will be recalled that the earlier resolution dealt mainly with a contributory old age insurance program and that as well contained certain amendments to the Old Age Security Act to provide for the payment of adjusted pensions beginning at any age from 65 years onward. The resolution now before us provides in addition for the payment of supplementary benefits for widows and orphans of contributors, and benefits to contributors who become disabled. This, of course, represents an important new dimension in the Canada pension plan.
I should like to recite some of the history in regard to this matter in order to freshen the recollection of members of the committee. Soon after Bill No. C-75 was presented earlier in this calendar year, during this session of the house, the government of the province of Quebec exposed the details of its own proposed pension plan. When these details were exposed it was clear that the Canada pension plan as incorporated in Bill No. C-75 and the proposed Quebec legislation were much closer in detail than had been anticipated at one time. Many of the features of the Quebec plan as revealed at Quebec city attracted favourable comment from provincial representatives who were there. Clearly there was a common goal that there should be a national contributory plan, and as a result of that consensus a series of negotiations were then undertaken to reach that common goal.
As I mentioned, one of the features found most attractive in the Quebec plan was the provision of supplementary benefits mentioned as desirable by government speakers from the beginning but which were not incorporated in Bill No. C-75 for reasons of which hon. members are aware. However, at Quebec city and subsequently all provincial representatives agreed that these features would have to be included in a truly comprehensive scheme.
Hon. members of this committee know full well that under the British North America Act, federal jurisdiction in this area is confined to pensions for the aged, and it was quite clear that if we wished to be able to add benefits of this kind to a comprehensive national scheme we would have to have an amendment to the constitution. Indeed, the previous government had at one time sought approval for such an amendment.

Not very long after that, agreement was reached on the phraseology of an amendment to be presented. This resolution was presented to the house by my colleague, the Minister of Justice, was approved, transmitted to Westminster, and in due course passed there. That amendment meant that the jurisdiction which was provided under section 94A of the B.N.A. Act was extended in order to cover supplementary benefits as well as old age pensions.
Before going into a closer examination of some of the provisions in the bill I would like to draw hon. members' attention to a new and important development. It will be recalled that in the earlier bill, Bill No. C-75, there was provision to base pensions on current earnings levels. That approach has been retained in the new bill and, in addition, provision has been made for an upward adjustment of benefits if living costs rise.
Throughout, one of the criticisms made of the earlier bill was that it failed to provide for our elderly citizens already in receipt of pensions. Indeed, the Canada pension plan, as opposed to the amendments to the Old Age Security Act, which are also incorporated in the bill, following September last year was never intended to provide anything for those now in pension. It will be recalled that the original intent was that there be a $10 supplementary payment made to one million odd old age pensioners from the proceeds of the Canada pension plan. When it was made clear by the province of Quebec in August of 1963 that it would produce its own plan, legislation was introduced and passed with the approval of all hon. members, to increase pensions to $75 a month, without waiting to go on with the Canada pension plan.
Since that time a number of representations have been made to the government, not the least being remarks made by interested hon. members in this chamber. Therefore we have provided under the new Canada pension plan, in addition to the $10 increase which was granted just over a year ago, that all future old age security pensions will be pegged to the cost of living index and will increase automatically if living costs increase.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
This is a new departure in old age security. It is in response to the oft heard cry of those in receipt of pensions that they are unable to keep up with their own expenses if the cost of living rises as they have to depend on intermittent pension payments which may be raised at any time or may be held down to a certain level for some
Canada Pension Plan
years. We hope, and I know this feeling will be shared by members in all corners of the chamber, that this will provide not only a greater measure of security but will also protect the real value of the pension dollar for Canada's million-odd pensioners.
The Canada pension plan as described in this resolution provides, as I said, for supplementary benefits and this makes it a truly comprehensive social insurance measure. Up until this time we have in Canada used the social assistance approach as the principal means of aiding survivors and disabled persons. As hon. members know, since world war I there has been provided in the provinces the kind of legislation known as mothers' allowances to help out widows who have dependant children. In recent years the federal and provincial governments have cooperated to provide assistance as well to the disabled. But these are welfare programs based on a test of need or means.
This plan, the Canada pension plan, is one which provides help as of right rather than on a need or a means test, for those who suffer the loss of a loved breadwinner or those who find themselves disabled and unable to carry on work. I think hon. members will agree this is a giant step forward in Canada's social security program.
These disability benefits under the Canada pension plan will provide help in family crises when it is most needed. When the head of a family dies and leaves his widow with young children, she will be provided with a pension to help her through those difficult years. A widow 35 years old or over, even though she has no dependant children, as hon. members know, often finds it difficult to re-enter the labour force and obtain work. There is provision for a pension for her; and the older she is and thus the less likely to be self-supporting, the greater her need and therefore the higher is her pension. Nor have the orphans of contributors been forgotten. They will be entitled to draw a benefit, generally until they join the work force.
Then in addition-and this is a new feature -upon the death of any contributor a payment will be made to his estate, whether or not there is a survivor's benefit payable.
For those who become disabled there is at least the comfort of knowing that a pension will be payable, on a temporary or on a permanent basis as needed. This pension is also available to a disabled widow or widower.
While one basic change in the program now to be considered is the fact that it is broader in scope by the provision of these supple-

Canada Pension Plan
mentary benefits, the other important development is that the program in fact will be truly national in its application, whether administered by the federal government or by a provincial government. The plan will operate uniformly across the country, and rights to benefit under it will be completely portable from sea to sea. As such we have every reason to believe that it will prove an important instrument in reinforcing our national unity as Canadians.
In a country such as ours which has such a high degree of mobility of manpower, the desirability of one common approach to pension legislation is readily apparent. This was one of the key points stressed during the negotiations already referred to, particularly by the head of the government of Ontario.
Through the long months of federal-provincial discussions leading to the bill which this resolution precedes, most of the best features of the proposed Quebec plan and of the Canada pension plan have been incorporated into this new program, along with a number of suggestions put forward by the other provinces and by various groups in their representations to the federal government.
One of the important changes from Bill No. C-75 is the extension of coverage of the selfemployed on a compulsory rather than voluntary basis. Last year submissions were made to the Canadian government by a number of bodies, including the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which made its submission on February 26. At that time that body asked that farmers be covered on a compulsory baeis. Several of the provincial premiers at the meetings which we have had also indicated concern that farmers and fishermen, ordinarily at the lower end of the earnings scale in many provinces, would not be adequately protected if coverage were left as entirely voluntary. The Quebec report favoured the approach of involuntary coverage, and that is the one followed in the old age and survivors' insurance program in the United States.
It will be clear that good arguments can be advanced for either approach, but on balance it appears in Canada there is a much broader support for the approach now incorporated in the new Canada pension plan. It is apparent that in this and in many other aspects of the program there will, of course, be honest differences as to whether one approach or course is better than another. But a great effort has been made to develop a program which will receive general acceptance by Canadians, knowing that in any plan which is as complex and attempts to be as compre-
[Miss LaMarsh.l
hensive as this one there will be some reservations on one point or another.
There is another change. The level of benefits provided for retirement is higher in the new bill than under Bill No. C-75. This was indicated in the white paper which hon. members have had a chance to study since August, and it will be noted when they see the new bill. This higher level of benefits has resulted from an adjustment of the maximum pensionable earnings and of the percentage of those earnings which was used to calculate the amount of the retirement benefit. This means that a maximum monthly retirement benefit of $104.17 is now proposed. This, combined with a maximum old age security payment of $75 a month, will make the over-all maximum pension $179.17 at age 70. I hope this increase in benefit will commend itself to all hon. members. Some will say it is too-low; others will say it is too high. However, we have balanced as carefully as we could all of the factors involved-Canadian wage levels, our economy, the cost of living and so forth

and on balance we decided that this represents the most reasonable benefit provision. The figure I quoted is, of course, the maximum and it is perfectly true that many people will receive somewhat less, depending, naturally, on the amount of contribution they have made in the course of their working lives.
For the average contributor, there is another change. The new program now envisaged being a richer one, there is a somewhat higher rate of contribution required. This higher rate of contribution will make it possible not only to finance the more generous retirement benefit, and the new survivors' and disability benefits, but will also result in higher investment reserves. These reserves will be made available for investment in obligations of provincial governments or of any agent of Her Majesty in the right of a province if that is guaranteed by the province. There will be interest on these reserves which are utilized by the provinces and this interest will go to the credit of the Canada pension plan and help finance it. These funds, moreover, will be very helpful to the provinces in the development of their social capital for such purposes as schools, roads, sewers, and hydroelectric projects, as well as for such developments as may desired in the provinces in the field of health and welfare, all in accordance with the scale of priorities of the provinces themselves.
The proposed legislation will also deal with the question of safeguards to the provinces,

and restraints in relation to future changes in the Canada pension plan. If the federal legislation dealt with a matter exclusively within federal jurisdiction, such provisions would not have been included. In fact, however, as hon. members know, parliament's power to legislate pensions is subject to the limitation that it must not affect present or future provincial laws. This gives to the provinces a legitimate day to day interest in the Canada pension plan, now, as well as in the future.
Special attention has been given to fulfilling the need for the closest possible coordination between the Quebec plan and the Canada pension plan. Suppose, for instance, a contributor has been paying into the plan in Quebec while he lived and worked there, and that he later went to live and work in another province where he paid into the Canada pension plan. From which authority will he draw his payments when he retires? When his pension becomes payable, under an agreement we have worked out with the Quebec authorities, he will receive one cheque to cover his total benefits; it will not matter to him where he worked-whether he stayed in one place all his life or whether he moved across the country. The act will determine which of the two jurisdictions will pay the pension and there will, of course, be provision for reimbursement from one to the other. It will be obvious that arrangements of this kind are essential for the highest possible co-ordination between the two plans, and this has resulted in a bill containing 125 clauses, a bill which is long and extremely complex.
When the bill goes to the joint parliamentary committee which it is proposed to establish, members of this committee will have before them, in addition to the white paper and the bill, actuarial and economic studies of the Canada pension plan for their information. When hon. members have a chance to see the bill this evening and when the public as a whole becomes familiar with the provisions of the new pension plan I feel sure the measures will receive a warm response-certainly it will be warmer in some places than in others-from almost all in the country.
It seems to me we are taking today a most important stride toward social security in our country, a stride of which all Canadians may be justly proud. It is one which is intended to provide not only an opportunity for the individual to help save for his own future dignity but also to help him provide for those who are normally dependant upon
Canada Pension Plan
him. I hope it will do much to bring not only members of the House of Commons together, members of this committee and of the special committee, but that it will do much to bring together all Canadians working under one plan to provide for their own and one another's security.

When she rose to make her statement to the committee, the minister I noticed received very warm applause. I was pleased this was the case because I knew she would need this encouragement after so many previous ill-fated efforts.
I believe the hon. lady indicated that the supplementary payments to which she referred had been urged on previous occasions by her own supporters. My recollection is that speakers from the government side of the house mentioned those supplementary payments only very occasionally in the course of previous debates; that it was, actually, opposition speakers who pressed for a recognition of the need in this regard.
I was very pleased to hear the minister's statement concerning a cost of living index adjustment to present recipients of old age security payments. This is a matter about which we have been greatly concerned in the past-something which was completely ignored in previous efforts.
I wish, now, to reiterate the stand I took on March 17 last when I stated that the party to which I belong is in favour of a Canada pension plan. Let there be no misunderstanding. The Progressive Conservative party- the government in power at that time- started this whole program rolling back in 1958. We have always stood for this type of guarantee, for this type of guarantee against fear for our older citizens as old age creeps on. At least the government has seen fit to bring in a plan which includes many of the additional benefits we have always advocated.
I ask, first of all: Why is this resolution before us? I believe that on a previous occasion-I do not recall whether it was in reply to a question by myself or not-the minister indicated that there were preliminary administrative costs which were being borne out of the general revenue prior to the actual inception of the plan? Am I right in that supposition? In other words, all the administrative expenses having to do with the Canada pension plan, present and future, are being met out of contributions. If that is the case I do not see why this resolution is before us at all-there is no expenditure involved by the government-unless it is to

Canada Pension Plan
justify what might be considered another tax. I do not see any other reason for it.
I understood the minister to say that the committee is not going to be set up until after the bill receives second reading. I would plead with the minister to reconsider this course. I really and honestly believe that a proper consideration, examination and study of representations from people across Canada should be made on the Canada pension plan and on the bill which is coming forward, which I understand contains 125 sections, and that to achieve this it would be much wiser to send this bill to committee before it receives second reading. If we go through second reading the government becomes committed to certain clauses which may, in the long run, if this matter is sent to committee, be proven ineffective; it might be proven that the bill would be better off without them. I know the minister will say that if this is the decision of the committee she will be very happy to give consideration to possible changes. I think that right from the first time a pension plan was put before us on July 18, 1963, there were indications both from the Prime Minister and the minister that they would study recommendations made, and so on; but I think good faith would be proven if this bill went to the special committee before it actually received second reading and the government's position became hardened and more difficult of adjustment. I would like to ask the minister -she may reply now or at any time-whether she proposes to have this committee set up and operating before Christmas.
The minister gave some of the history of the Canada pension plan. I believe the history she gave started with the conference in Quebec and I would like to give a little of the previous history. We all recall that on July 18, 1963, the first version was brought before us, and we also recall the very political approach taken by the minister at that time.

Yes, they voted against the recipients of old age security receiving this increase. There was a level of $4,000 maximum income. The blind, disabled and those receiving old age assistance were completely ignored at that time; and there was no opting out by provinces. There was issued a white paper giving a supplementary outline of the scheme presented to us. I could mention what I believe were some excellent advances made by the previous government in the health and welfare field, including the start of the actual Canada pension plan which we are seeing here today; however, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to do that because my time is limited.
I would, however, continuing the historical angle of this plan, mention that when we came back on September 30, 1963, the government had not prepared the business for the session. This matter first came before us on July 18, 1963, and due to our insistence it was subsequently finally agreed that an amendment be brought forward for an increase of $10 per month in old age security. However, at that time the blind, disabled and those receiving old age assistance were still excluded from the increase. We were certainly in favour of this increase and we voted for it. But what was the price to the taxpayer? The government had in their election literature indicated that this was going to be financed

Canada Pension Plan
out of the contributions to the Canada pension plan; but instead of that the taxpayers across Canada today are paying something over $100 million extra in taxes.
I mentioned earlier that the minister was very humble on March 17. That day the resolution preceding Bill No. C-75 was passed and the bill was given first reading. Then, as the minister mentioned, the Quebec conference took place and Quebec unveiled their plan. Apparently after the conference was over there was some really high pressured wheeling and dealing going on for a period of days at least; I understand there were several meetings. Then eventually a compromise was announced as between the Quebec plan and the government's plan. On April 20, 1964, the Prime Minister tabled letters to the provinces asking for consent to amend the British North America Act, and this was eventually received. Now we have the third version before us. On March 17 last I asked the minister whether those were to be the minister's last confident words on this pension plan. I did so because of the boastful but completely incompetent presentation which she had brought forward on July 18. Events certainly proved me to be correct in asking her at that time. I am sure she thought they were her last words, but events proved otherwise.

speechtext:
I hope the future holds for this plan the very best of everything. We want to see it in committee and we want to get it there fast.
I have read, Mr. Chairman, all the material available, and in particular the white paper. I should like to ask the minister, because I do not doubt that this question will be raised later in the debate, whether she has given proper consideration to any conflict with the Hall health report and the extra cost involved in this pension plan. I do not suggest that she has to answer but I am wondering, had she received the Hall report concerning health services before having embarked on the pension plan, which one she would have chosen. Or would she have chosen both? Certainly it would be to the advantage of all Canadians to choose both; but at the same time I suppose the Minister of Finance has put some brakes on the minister, and I also expect that the finance officials will be before the committee when it is set up.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in referring to the white paper may I say that the necessary amendment to section 94A of the British
North America Act has certainly made this a worth-while plan in comparison with the plans put before us before. You will recall that the government of which the Leader of the Opposition had the honour to be the head had attempted to get this particular amendment passed, but had not been able to do so. However, under this new plan widows under 65 years of age and their dependants, and the disabled, are going to receive benefits which were not possible previously. There is a section entitled "Main features of the pensions" on page 7 of the white paper. These provisions can hardly be recognized from the previous efforts. With regard to timing, retirement pensions will begin in January 1967. This is, of course, a year later than had previously been anticipated by the minister and promised on July 18, 1963.
There is one point which disturbs me, Mr. Chairman, and it is this. I am not prepared at the moment to say that this is not the correct thing to do, although surely study in committee will clear the point up somewhat. The self-employed will be compulsorily included in the plan. This means that an average of 3.6 per cent of all earnings by self-employed workers will be paid into this plan-not 1.8 per cent as with employed persons, but 3.6 per cent. I think this is going to be found quite a drain on the capacities of various self-employed people and I think it is a matter which will have to be looked at. With regard to adjustments for increases in the cost of living, as I said earlier we were very pleased to see that the minister has included a cost of living adjustment for those receiving old age security. This was a woeful omission from previous presentations.
However, there is one class of person who I think should be considered in this matter. I heard a young fellow of 18 years say the other day, Mr. Chairman: "I am going to pay into this pension plan for 52 years and not get one cent more out of it than the person who has been paying into it for ten years". I know there is a cost of living adjustment and so on, but that is the fact and I think our young people will look at this.
Then there is a section headed "Adjustment for earnings after retirement". It indicates that pensions can be reduced if a person has earned income of over $900 a year, no matter from what source it may come. For example, a person might retire from a job and then become self-employed after the age of 70 and make $900 a year. He will therefore have his pension reduced.

Canada Pension Plan
I see my time is up. May I say there are many changes for which we have asked earlier affecting disability pensions, widows under 65 years of age, disabled persons and so on. I should like to know how many provinces are actually committed to the scheme.
There is one other section I should like to mention in relation to other retirement plans. This whole section rather blandly assumes that integrating existing private pension plans with the Canada pension plan will not be a great problem. I suggest that it is in this area that most of our immediate headaches are going to arise. I suggest that consideration should be given to allowing public plans, such as the civil service superannuation plan and those private plans which are of exceptional standard, to remain out of the Canada pension plan. My purpose in suggesting this is because we do not want to see any individual's pension or pension arrangements suffer as a result of this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, we welcome the introduction of this resolution and we are prepared to welcome the bill which will be introduced at the end of this day's sitting. I confess that it gets a bit difficult to express one's welcome with the same warmth after he has done it two or three times already; but despite the tarnish that time may have put upon the proposed Canada pension plan it is still true that we are launching upon a piece of legislation which is extremely important in terms of improving the lot of all of the people of this country.
Some of the things one might say on this occasion need not be said because they were said on July 18 of last year or March 17 of this year. Therefore, perhaps the minister can take as read the fact that we are glad to have this plan back again. We are glad to have the improvements which were indicated in the white paper which was tabled in August, and we are glad to hear of the two or three additional improvements that the minister announced today.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps the thing that needs most to be said at this time should be directed not just to the Minister of National Health and Welfare but to the government as a whole. What is most needed is that this legislation get passed at this session, and it has a long way to go. Thanks to the new rule under which we are operating, the debate at this stage can last only for this day. But the bill still has to go through second reading, to the special committee which is to be appointed, and it then has to come back to the committee of the whole house, and then

go through the third reading stage. We are already away over time in this session, and no one knows how long it is going to last.
I am still relying on the undertaking that the Minister of Justice gave on July 6, at which time he was the government house leader. He made it clear that the government would see to it that the completion of the legislative process with respect to the Canada pension plan would be effected before the end of the present session. It was for that reason the leader of this party, earlier this afternoon, urged that second reading of the Canada pension plan be given priority above the motions for concurrence in the reports of the special committee on the flag. I suggest to the government that if it puts the flag debate-which may last for a number of days-
