and then moving on to the Columbia river project, they must carry their retirement plans with them.
It should be noted that construction workers do not work the year round every year. They, like so many others, have their excellent years and their bad years. Therefore I believe it is fitting that the retirement benefits will be based on average earnings over a lifetime, with adjustments being made for the lean years and the overly good years.
Construction workers are just one segment of the working force of Canada that must face the problems arising out of being highly mobile men. Automation too is going to change the picture and location of many in the labour force of this nation. As more and more jobs become automated the need for skilled technicians to move in and get a project started is going to increase. These technicians are going to be a highly skilled mobile training force and their number will grow. They will need portable pensions.
I should like to digress for a moment to point out that the city of Sarnia in my riding is regarded as the most highly automated city in Canada. As the major petroleum and chemical industries located there automated, men were gradually processed out of jobs. I do not mean to imply that they were fired, to be replaced by machines. They continued on the job but as they reached retirement age they were pensioned off and quite handsomely too. The point I am making is that the city of Sarnia has automated and the phasing out of the labour force was handled without any major dislocation.
But as the process of automation is speeded up, so will be the phasing out of older workers and in some cases they will not be as fortunate as the people in my riding who worked for firms that provided pensions. They will find themselves out of a job with no visible means of support. They will swell the unemployment rolls. They will become the ancient mariners of our land, stopping passers-by to tell their tale of woe.
The Canada pension plan could forestall this by assuring them of an adequate income. They would not have to seek full time employment. Their many skills would be available to fill the gaps where part time help is needed. I think it is only right that this bill should contain provisions enabling a retired person to take on a part time job if he or she feels it is worth while. None of us likes to feel he is not needed. We all like to feel we are required and that we are useful and can do something meaningful. The legislation

under debate here recognizes this fact, with its provisions to allow a retired person to continue to contribute his skills to a limit which he himself can determine.
For all these reasons, for the dignity of old age, for the reward of a lifetime of toil, to enable the generation even now moving into the work field to find employment, to help ease the transition to automation, to make all Canada a market for a man's skills, to create capital for the further development of our resources but, above all, Mr. Chairman, because we all know we have a duty in conscience to care for the aged and the elderly, I urge upon the house the necessity for the speedy passage of this legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. It is my duty, pursuant to provisional standing order 3 9A, to inform the house that the questions to be raised at ten o'clock p.m. this day are as follows:
The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp), re feeder cattle prices; the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler), re the depressed position of eastern farmers.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset I should like to compliment the minister on finally getting this compulsory, contributory pension plan before us. I am sure it has been a trying period for her in being held back so much in her attempts to bring forth this major piece of legislation. I should like to tell her I enjoyed listening to her this afternoon, and may I say her reasonable, quiet approach became her.
I was also pleased to listen to my close personal friend, the hon. member for Lamb-ton West, who painted a beautiful picture of this plan, and I compliment him on a worthy presentation. Now I know why he was so successful in his previous business. I am in agreement with much of what he said, but in my opinion there are certain areas of this matter which should be examined under a bright light.
We all share the hope that this plan is more realistic, more palatable and a little more down to earth than were the previous ones. The white paper gives us a brief outline of the plan but of course it is couched

in the language of a well prepared sales brochure. In other words, it does not give too much actual detail but concentrates on glowing, descriptive features of the plan. I look forward to seeing the actual bill and to examining it very soon.
I was delighted to learn of our flat rate pension scheme being tied in with the cost of living index, but in my discussion of the resolution tonight I would like to examine it in the light of priorities. What should we do first? What are the social requirement priorities of Canada at present? What is the most important social action at this time? Is it on pensions? Is it on health or education?
The royal commission on health services has pointed out that by 1971 we will be spending $466 million annually on health services, and in addition that we will need $400 million for expansion of and additions to medical schools. In the light of this I propose to discuss what priorities should be undertaken.
So far as I am concerned the role of the federal government in social security should be to provide a floor for universal retirement, to provide a level below which no Canadian is forced or allowed to go. In this connection I pay tribute to our flat rate plan. It is expensive in its cost but it is cheap to administer. It is not related to status in life but is universally available.
I suggest improvements could be made in it. So far as old age security is concerned I believe our most effective step at this time would be to update the present plan, and as the minister mentioned this is being done to a certain degree. I believe it should be modernized, modified and overhauled. I believe the qualifying age should be reduced from 70 to 65 years, but the plan should be administered on an actuarial basis. I even go so far as to suggest that at normal retirement age of 65, when a husband proves he has withdrawn from the work force, his wife should receive her pension, and her pension could be easily adjusted to take into account any great disparity in age.
Quite a case can be made for the proposition that the older a person is the larger his pension should be. A bigger flat rate pension should be provided for those aged 80, and 85 years, because in many instances older people have had to spend their savings for extra help in the home and extra doctors' bills. In many cases the needs of people in this age group are greater than the needs of people aged 70 or 75 who may be able to look after themselves better.
Canada Pension Plan
I would favour a pension commission or board completely removed from politics, a board set up to administer the flat rate pension related to average earnings or, as the minister has already announced, related to the cost of living index.
There are great variations of conditions between the vast areas of this great country and in my opinion local conditions can best be met by local or regional governments. Therefore I propose that a modernization of our flat rate pension plan be considered first. I do not think I am completely alone in this view. For seven years the Canadian welfare council has said that other social schemes have priority. I do not say this is necessarily correct, but let us discuss this question openly and find out. We have only so much by way of resources to dispose of, and the setting up of a list of priorities should, I believe, be considered. I submit that the real order of priority in this country would probably be: education, medicare, and then pensions.
I personally favour a pay as you go scheme, a plan which does not build up huge funds to be administered by politicians. These pension funds are trust funds; I might even go as far as to say they are sacred trust funds, and they should never be under the control of politicians. Look at the list of investments for which these funds may be used. The provinces have the right to use these moneys and if they do not need them the remainder can be invested in dominion government securities. I deplore this method of looking after trust funds. I pay tribute to our life insurance companies and insurance companies generally for having done such a good job in this regard. I would prefer that trained, highly skilled investment experts removed from political considerations should have control over the investment features of any pension fund in which I was involved.
I am also concerned about the very high cost of administration which this plan will necessitate. The career of every citizen from the age of 18 to the age of 70 will have to be followed in the minutest detail. It will be a repetition of the experience of the business community-the Department of Industry at the front door and the department of inland revenue at the back door. Just look at how the numbers of civil servants have increased in recent years. I submit that the benefits flowing from this plan are not commensurate with the cost and will not make up for the ill effects of the disruption of existing plans. As I see it, the plan subsidizes those who are in least need; its greatest benefits accrue to

Canada Pension Plan
those who need them least. A welfare plan should take care of those who really need assistance. I think the people should be told the truth. All that a pension plan is, is money -money for future delivery. The government has no magic formula for administering pension funds better than anyone else. As far as I can see there is no economy which can be effected by federal administration as opposed to existing facilities. The only thing a government can do is to make it compulsory for everybody to belong.
According to the white paper, this plan provides nothing for people who are now over 70, though many of these people really need additional help. Further, it provides little for those who are over the age of 65. Finally, it does not look to me like much of a bargain for those who are 25 or under, because they will be paying for many years and getting no more out of the plan than a man who is 55 years of age.
I further suggest that those who need pensions most, as a class, are those who are engaged in seasonal pursuits-trappers, fishermen, construction workers, and so on. Taking into account their limited incomes, this plan offers little real benefit to them. Farmers and the self-employed are, I submit, being penalized. It is true that farmers can participate, as can other groups of self-employed people, but they must pay the whole shot. Groups of employees in industry pay approximately one half of the contribution made in respect of them; the employer pays approximately the same amount. This is, in truth, a payroll tax. The extra cost of doing business, the extra cost of production brought about as a result of the employer contribution must in large measure be passed along to the consumer. So I submit the farm people and the selfemployed who constitute a large segment of the economy of this country will be paying their full share, plus a bonus to the others in the form of higher prices for goods and services. I think this is unfair. I am not alone in this belief, because a former minister of transport, appearing before the joint committee, had this to say about the same question:
I think it is pretty clear that a tax on wages and salaries would have a very direct effect on cost of production. I would think if there were a payroll tax, paid by the employer, the tendency would be for it to be passed on in prices almost immediately.
Rest assured, this is a payroll tax. I suggest the self-employed and the farm people would be much better off under a modernized, up to date flat rate plan. This I submit would

go a long way toward alleviating hardship in the depressed areas.
On the basis of irregular earnings the pension, as I mentioned a few moments ago, amounts to little or nothing. On the whole it provides for those who are not in dire need. Let us consider one or two other points. In industry, contributory pensions have been a matter for union bargaining. Several union leaders have already stated that they would not consider the integration of existing plans with this new, compulsory Canada pension plan. I foresee labour-management disputes which will put an additional burden on business and on the economy in general. Some of our provincial governments are now concerned with legislation covering the portability of pensions within and between provinces. This is a matter which comes under provincial jurisdiction. If such arrangements are made, what excuse is there for imposing this scheme on a company which can prove that it has a plan equal to, or better than, the one proposed by the government? In 1950 the type of plan now put forward was turned down and the committee advocated a flat rate plan. Conditions change, I know, but by and large the same situation prevails today as prevailed then.
I deplore the fact that there is no factual actuarial report presented with this white paper-just an anonymous opinion that the economy can take the cost. It assumes a pension plan standing by itself and I submit the cost of the plan must be considered in toto, together with all the other costs of government. I quote Mr. John B. Meyer of the Montreal Gazette who on August 14, 1964 asked:
Can we really afford the claim upon income represented by the pension plan on top of present and future claims, particularly that represented by the recommendation of the royal commission on health services? This should be the starting point for any examination of the plan. It is ignored completely in the white paper.
Again, may I say a contributory compulsory plan is definitely worthy of consideration. I do not feel it is all bad; I think it can be overhauled and made to work. But I submit that, as usual, this government has given it the wrong priority. I suggest that a more appropriate priority would be to update and modernize our present plan, remove it from politics and then consider education, medicare and a contributory, compulsory pension plan, in that order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, today there is a tendency in this house and elsewhere, to men-

tion at every turn "the government's capitulating to the provinces'' and, more particularly " to Quebec", as there is-I am sorry to say, on the other hand frequent talk of "Quebec's yielding to Ottawa" in some Quebec groups.
These detestable expressions of "yielding", or "capitulating" will, I hope, not be used in respect of the pension plan which the Minister of National Health and Welfare introduced this afternoon.
If there is to be any talk of "capitulation", it will be, I hope, to common sense, a yielding to the need of compromise which should necessarily govern the solution of political problems and to the new spirit which marks federal-provincial relations at this time.
Mr. Chairman, how did we arrive at the present situation? How did we come to the pension plan such as it is today?
At the time where inevitably, fortunately and dangerously also was developing the technique of opting out and contracting out a new technique appeared, which I could called the contracting in formula, an agreement between the central government and one or several provinces upon the passing of similar legislation.
In order to remind you of these facts, Mr. Chairman, in July 1963 the central government initiated a pension scheme; it was certainly its right. Some provinces indicated their interest in moving into the same legislative field; it was also their right. Then complex and lengthy negotiations started; all the Cassandras of the country uttered a unanimous opinion: confederation is in danger; it is even already dead, assassinated, as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) would say.
After months of work during which politicians and federal and provincial officials did their best, a compromise was reached on a pension plan. In this atmosphere of optimism, a constitutional amendment was approved providing for benefits to survivors and disabled persons.
The provinces have two alternatives: they may either have their own plan or they may accept that of the central government. Essential parts of both plans are identical.
In short, those are the facts, Mr. Chairman. The proposed plan is a national plan, with all the benefits that this involves. It is a national plan without being exclusively a federal plan. It is national because it can be either a federal or a provincial plan; provinces can choose the federal plan or have their own provincial plan if they so wish.
Canada Pension Plan
For those who would be tempted in this debate to speak of concessions to provinces, to Quebec particularly, I would like first of all to reaffirm the priority rights of the provinces in the field of pension plans and, in the second place, indicate improvements to the federal plan following its merger, so to speak, with the Quebec plan.
For the others, that is those who would be tempted to say that this is a Quebec concession to Ottawa, I would like to mention the improvements made to the Quebec plan resulting from the merger with the original federal plan.
First, the constitutional aspect: as I said earlier, both the federal and provincial governments were perfectly entitled to introduce their own pension plan.
Section 94A, arising out of the amendment of 1951, and amended in 1964, reads as follows:
The parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pension in Canada, but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future-
I emphasize: present or future.
-of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions.
Because of that 1951 amendment the legislation on old age pensions had become a joint field like agriculture and immigration.
However, while in these two latter fields, section 95 grants a priority, a "paramountcy" to central legislation, section 94A recognizes the paramountcy of the provincial legislation, not only for the existing law, but for any future provincial law.
As soon as the provincial legislation is affected in relation to pension plans, the federal government must withdraw. This is provided by the constitution.
Therefore, I think it was impossible to have federal and provincial plans, both being government comprehensive plans.
I conclude and I think that this conclusion must be kept in mind during this debate: the federal government was not free to do as it pleases as regards pension plans. It had, and it has to agree with the provinces. It had and it has to do so in order to give the pension plan all the desirable scope, stability and efficiency.
An agreement was therefore achieved through the constructive will of the central government and through the good will of the provinces and of Quebec particularly.
The minister will be accused-it was done already this afternoon-of having attacked,

Canada Pension Plan
of having retreated, having amended, having altered. This afternoon, the Leader of the Opposition grumbled:	Two revisions, two
revisions.
The minister would have been accused of the opposite if an agreement had not been reached.
It would have been said then that she had lacked flexibility. It would have been said then that she was in favour of centralization.
The people will take all that into consideration and that is why they will not take away from the Minister of National Health and Welfare the popularity she now enjoys.
What has been the influence of the Quebec plan on the evolution of the final federal plan, a summary of which was given to us this afternoon? You understand that it would be necessary here to compare the two original plans, the Quebec plan and the final federal plan. I do not have enough time and I will limit myself to a few points.
First, in addition to remaining a social security plan, the present plan also becomes a source of capital. It has often been said that for the people of Quebec who want to have a hand in their own economic development, capitalization was essential, and I think we must congratulate the federal government and the other provinces for having understood that. I feel that the other provinces will also benefit from this change.
Second, "coverage", that is the number of assessable persons, has also grown. Such exceptions as the dependent workers, originally considered, have been set aside. Participation of self-employed workers, optional in the original plan, now becomes compulsory, as it is in the Quebec plan. Revenue will obviously be increased, as will the benefits. Had selfemployed workers been free to join the plan or not, only those with fairly high income would have done so and the social security aspect would have suffered therefrom.
Third, the assessable income is set at a minimum of $600 and a maximum of $5,000. You will remember that the original federal plan foresaw from zero to $4,500, while the Quebec plan provided for $1,000 to $6,000. The compromise of $600 will have for effect, we must say, to benefit the less fortunate people, since a person who, for instance, is paying benefits or contributions on $1,400 will receive an annuity based on $2,000, since the exemption will not be deducted for the calculation of benefits.
Fourth, the contribution rate has been increased. In the first federal plan it was 2 per cent at the beginning. It must be pointed out

also that it increased up to 4 per cent for salaried people and up to 3 per cent in the case of self-employed workers. Under the provincial plan, the basis was 4 per cent indefinitely. Under the present plan, the basis is 3.6 per cent of the contributive revenue of the self-employed worker. It is 1.8 per cent for the employee, and 1.8 per cent for the employer in the case of dependent workers.
But take heed. Because of the basic exemption of $600, the rate is, in fact, less than 3.6 per cent. Especially, the rate is a progressive one. It is very low for the small wage earner, i.e., 1.4 per cent in the case of an employee earning $2,000; the rate increasing as the earnings increase. I think the social security aspect will greatly benefit from it. As far as the economic aspect is concerned, it is also worth while, because the small employer will pay less than large industries, their employees receiving ordinarily smaller salaries than those employed in larger industries.
Fifth, the expected retirement benefits of 20 per cent are raised to 25 per cent and will be adjusted, as in the Quebec plan, according to a formula which is a compromise in itself. Its advantage is obvious.
Sixth, the original federal plan could not, in the absence of a constitutional amendment, provide for payments to "non-old" survivors. With regard to the transfer of the pension to the disabled, to the widow, to the orphan, as far as death benefits are concerned, the final plan follows-improving on it at times- the Quebec plan.
Once again, I must say that undoubtedly, without the compromise arrived at, the provinces, especially the province of Quebec, would not have approved the constitutional amendment obtained last summer. I feel that must be recalled.
Seventh, an adjustment formula concerning the minimum and maximum of the assessable income and the benefits themselves is added to the original federal plan, taking into consideration the cost of living to begin with and later on the index of salaries.
That formula is itself a compromise, but the idea to adjust benefits comes, I have been told, from the Quebec plan. The idea is of undeniable value since its result is to maintain the purchasing power of the pension, in periods of inflation, obviously.
Finally, a last improvement: the administration of the plan is improved; all sorts of compromises concerning, for instance, the appeal procedure, the inclusion of federal and provincial civil servants, have also been secured. Is that convincing enough? I believe

Canada Pension Plan
so. The federal plan benefits from its association with the Quebec plan. I would like to add also that the Quebec plan gains a lot from its association with the federal plan.
First of all, the date when benefits will be available is moved ahead, the transitory period is reduced from 20 to 10 years. Thus the services rendered the country by the persons who have now reached somewhat advanced maturity can be recognized.
Second, the amount of exemption is reduced to $600 from $1,000. This will allow participation to this pension plan by a greater number of those in the low-income bracket.
Third, benefits to the disabled, which were reserved for persons of 60 years of age or more in the Quebec plan, will not be available, after five years of contributions, to anyone 23 years old or more.
Once again, and I now conclude to allow the member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau) to be recognized, this is a compromise. In a compromise each party loses a little, but each also gains more.
Both the federal and the provincial plans are better than before April 1964. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) admitted that fact only a few hours ago.
And above all, Mr. Chairman, the whole of Canada is better off after the events I just mentioned. First, we have at last a pension plan. Then-and I think it is important-I feel that a new technique has been invented in the field of federal-provincial relations, which I called a while ago "contracting in," namely the agreement of the federal government and the provinces in order to pass together identical legislation.
Finally, this pension plan, which is another great achievement in the realm of cooperative federalism, proves once more the maturity of Canadian political leaders.

Mr. Chairman, there is
hardly a person in this house who does not approve of a pension plan which will support those who need that support in old age, or in the cases of need that precedes old age. This being so one wonders why there was so much opposition to the plans previously suggested. The minister says that there are important new dimensions in the plan now. We are glad to hear this. It is hardly necessary to repeat that the opposition originally was not to the basic principles of a pension but to the failure properly to implement these principles in the first two schemes.
Now that this scheme has been hammered out by the opposition and been refined in the furnace of controversy, it begins to be a good plan. However, I think there are certain warnings that still need to be given and certain facts that it would be well for the people of this country to know and understand.
The basic principle of the plan is indicated in this quotation which I take from the government's white paper of August 1964, page 7:
Adequate levels of pensions cannot be realistically achieved, in a country like Canada, simply by increasing the flat-rate pension. Living costs vary greatly between town and country, and between different regions of Canada. What people need, if either retirement or the death or disablement of the head of the family removes their regular income, is related in part to the level of earnings to which they have been accustomed.
The Canada pension plan will therefore provide a retirement pension related to the earnings on which people have contributed. The scale of this pension will rise during a ten year transitional period to a level of 25 per cent of these earnings.
This is a good principle and one, I am sure, with which we all agree. However, we should not be carried away by this statement. It leaves the impression that a retiree will get 25 per cent of his earnings when he retires. This is only true with certain important qualifications. Some get more and some get less.
In fact, those whose earnings are below $5,000 yearly will at the end of the transitional period of ten years, and if the person retiring is 70 years of age, be paid 25 per cent of earnings on the earnings related pension, and on that alone. They will as well receive a further $75 a month from the old age security pension. A man then who earns $200 monthly would receive $50 earnings related pension plus $75 old age security pension, a total of $125 a month. This is 62 per cent of his previous monthly wage, and it is not a bit too much. The man earning $5,000 a year gets $416.67 monthly wage. His earnings related pension would be $104.17 monthly plus the old age security pension of $75, a total of $179.17. This is only 43 per cent of his previous monthly wage. The man earning $10,000 a year gets $833.34 monthly wage. His earnings related pension and old age security pension are the same as the man earning $5,000 a year, or again a total of $179.17. This is only 21J per cent of his previous monthly wage.
Thus this earnings related pension and the old age security pension are providing, as a little further calculation will show, at incomes below $8,600, a pension which is 25 per cent

Canada Pension Plan
or better of earnings prior to retirement. This is little enough since many pension plans strive to provide 70 per cent to a certain arbitrary maximum, at earnings based on that figure of $8,600. This pension then provides a pension which in many cases is below 25 per cent of earned income.
However, since this is a minimum plan, this is not surprising, and I do not think we should criticize it on that basis. It was not my purpose to do so, but I think these facts should be brought out. In fact it is a good thing that a pension scheme should pay higher percentages to low income groups so that these people may have enough money with which to live in reasonable comfort. It is necessary for those who are now in other pension schemes to keep these variable percentages in mind when considering what course they should follow with their present schemes in relation to the Canada pension plan.
For many years I was much concerned with the pension scheme for my profession in the province of Saskatchewan. When that scheme was introduced it was a good scheme related to earnings, but the depression of the 1930's almost wrecked it and had to be drastically revised on other principles in 1942. With the rising cost of living and rising salaries after 1945 there were years of struggle to have major increases introduced into the scheme. In 1957 major increases were obtained, but as the cost of living and salaries continued to increase another major redrafting was done in 1963 and the pension plan went back to the principle of relation to income. I mention this only to emphasize that thinking in the pension field changes, with the hope that a flexible attitude will be taken by the government when the bill is referred to committee for detailed study, and also the hope that the government will willingly accept the necessary revisions that are almost certain to come out of that study.
I mention it as well for another reason, and I think a very important one. There are a great many very good pension schemes in operation in this country. They have been hammered out through the years with much debate, and not always good humoured debate, until today they tend to do what they set out to do-protect the employees they cover and provide adequate pensions. The costs to the employees and employers are quite appreciable, and are distinctly noticeable in the reductions they produce in the salary cheques of the employees covered, as anyone who has been covered by such a plan and who has had

deductions made from his salary cheque will realize.
The Canada pension plan is going to upset all the carefully planned arrangements these schemes have evolved and tested throughout the years, and I think it is going to be a great deal more difficult to talk to the government than it was to talk to the employer, when modifications were desirable. I hope that by providing pensions for those who were not covered before, the Canada pension plan is not going to upset these plans. I am very suspicious about this because we hear that the federal civil servants and provincial civil servants are not going to be covered by the Canada pension plan. At least that is what the Calgary Herald of October 20 stated, and I should like to quote from that newspaper as follows:
When the federal government first broached the idea of a Canada pension plan, It emphasized that that it would be a universal scheme to which all Canadians would be required to contribute.
Yet, at the very outset, an exception was conceded-federal civil servants would remain outside the federal scheme, and their own plan would remain in effect.
Now, it has been revealed that provincial civil servants will be able to opt out of the plan as well. This seems most unsatisfactory. By what right should only provincial and federal civil servants be permitted to opt out and carry on with their own schemes? If this has to be a universal, compulsory plan, there is no justification for giving favoured treatment to any section of the Canadian public.. .there are many other Canadians who are not public servants who also have been contributing for many years to private and company schemes which are far superior to that which Ottawa is determined to foist on the nation.
The minister said today that the act is to be "truly national in its provisions" and that it "will operate uniformly across the country". These are strange statements indeed, if the newspaper is correct. Are these people then not to be in the plan? If they are not, then why are they not? Is it because they know that their own plans are better? What then about all the private plans that are good, are they to opt out completely, as the civil servants are allowed to do? If they are not able to do this then why, if civil servants can, are others not allowed to do the same? What about the broad base needed to carry the plan? I hope that in the negotiations carried on with the administrators of these plans the government will not be dictatorial and arrogant. Perhaps I am unduly pessimistic, but if I am, this government has only itself to blame. Its mistakes have been legion and its arrogances obvious. If the government is to continue this attitude, they may find that the

Canada pension plan is not the vote catcher they think it is.
The self-employed and the small businessman, in which group I include the farmers of my constituency, are going to have trouble with this scheme. The self-employed has to make the employer's contribution of 1.8 per cent, and also the employee's contribution of 1.8 per cent, so he will be paying 3.6 per cent for coverage for himself under the plan. He is going to notice this, just as the salary pensioner is going to notice his increased payments. Most self-employed create an estate which they expect will maintain them when they retire. Creation of that estate will be more difficult, due to this loss of income to the pension fund. It may be argued that the businessman or farmer will get it back as pension. This is true, but will the government make that money produce for the farmer as well as he would make it produce for himself? We all know it will not. The government will probably just sit on it or put it into bonds, which is nice and safe but not very productive, especially for the small businessman.
And are we sure that the rate will not be increased? My experience with pension plans suggests that it will need to be increased and the experience of the United States with a very similar plan resulted in the rate there having to be increased. I will never forget how I listened with amazement when the minister told us in August, 1963 what the benefits of the then Canada pension plan would be and what the rates to pay for those benefits would be. We all know what has happened to the benefits and rates, the one down and the other up. In the Canada pension plan they now seem reasonable but if any pension plan is to continue to fulfil its function of adequately supporting the pensioner with some relation to income its benefits and its rates will have to rise as the country goes forward.
There is a cost of living clause built into the Canada pension plan now, which will help. Then the minister tells us today that a cost of living provision will be attached to the old age pension too, and so it should be. But I am as certain as a man can be that the rates will need to be raised if we are going to get better benefits, and we will need better benefits in time. Yet the minister says that there are restraints in the present plan to prevent changes in the rates and benefits. This seems to forecast a battle. However, if the rates do rise the farmer and the businessman as well as the employee are the people who are going to feel the increases.
20220-628J
Canada Pension Plan
These are the comments I should like to make at this time. I am all in favour of a good pension scheme and so is my party. They had a study under way when defeated in 1963. My party showed its concern for the pensioner, with the assistance of the other opposition groups, by forcing the government to meet its promise to pay $75 a month to the old age pensioners. This government had tied that increase to the Canada pension plan. The old age pensioners would still be waiting for it and would have been $120 poorer today if the government had carried out its intentions.

Mr. Chairman, it is a distinct honour for me to participate in this historic debate today. We know that for the past decade or so this country has been noticeably unimaginative in its attitude toward social security. Since universal old age pensions were introduced in 1952 we have had only one major piece of social security legislation introduced in the House of Commons, namely the hospital insurance legislation introduced some years ago.
During this period successive governments did increase the benefits, of course, available under existing programs but this required neither great courage nor imagination. However, there was little evidence, and there has been little evidence up until now of an evolution of a sound philosophy of social security. The nineteenth century attitude which from time to time prevails in criticizing social security has left a legacy of myths about social security and the welfare state which are not only erroneous but, it would seem, have restricted governments in the past from taking a more imaginative and realistic approach toward the social and economic problems of modern society.
The lack of a sound, balanced approach to social security is admittedly complicated by the federal nature of our society. It is this very set of circumstances which has in the past and will in the future present some severe tests to the federal government. The present administration is to be congratulated for surmounting some of the difficulties inherent in our federal system which complicate the problem of attaining national standards in pensions and in other fields.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the achievement of bringing forth a national contributory pension plan which is truly portable is a testimonial not only to the progressive spirit of the present administration but also to its ability to cope with the problems of a federal

Canada Pension Plan
state. This is all the more remarkable when we note that this was brought about by a government in a minority position in the House of Commons and at a time when there is a great deal of controversy centered around the House of Commons and around confederation itself.
In the past decade Canada had two governments which enjoyed overwhelming majorities in the House of Commons. Yet neither of these administrations took this very fundamental forward step of providing this very basic part of Canada's social security system, a step forward, Mr. Chairman, which more than any other is in my opinion a realization of the need for a sound philosophy of social security. In the past year or so the matter of a Canada pension plan has been discussed at four federal-provincial conferences. In view of the constitutional division of powers it was impossible for the federal government to proceed as completely as it now has in this field. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, what we have seen over the past year has been co-operative federalism at work. Because of the sound and reasonable approach taken by this administration to the matter of federal-provincial relations we now will have a national pension plan which provides for portability between all provinces, and we also have the necessary constitutional amendment to provide for supplementary pensions for widows, orphans and disabled contributors. Therefore this government has not only introduced a great social security measure but in doing so it has brought Canadians of all origins closer together by crossing what seemed a year ago to be insurmountable obstacles. It is a great tribute to this administration's ability to cope with the difficulties inherent in our present political environment. It is also a great rebuke to those purveyors of pessimism and proponents of instant wisdom who have severely criticized our democratic institutions.
That these are times of controversy no one will deny. It seems to me, however, that in times of great change one hears all too much of the negative side of things. It is perhaps easier to succumb to fear than to summon the courage to cope with the situation. Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, we pay far too much attention to the prophets of doom.
The events of the past year which led to the introduction of today's resolution can only confirm our conviction that the present administration is providing us with calm and reasonable leadership that refuses to be deterred from its course by extremism from any quarter. It represents a great triumph for
[Mr. Cashin.l
moderation over extremism and gives one confidence that men and women of reason can, with patience and understanding, arrive at a common consensus. It is a great lesson in the art of government.
The white paper on pensions tabled in August gives us a good indication of the scope and the magnitude of this legislation. There are two significant features which represent an improvement over the original plan and which were achieved through negotiations with the provinces over the past year. These negotiations, as I have said, are a vivid example of co-operative federalism at work. First of all, this is now a truly national plan which provides for complete portability from province to province. This is an important step in providing greater mobility within the labour force. Workers must be free to move from job to job anywhere in Canada. Now they will be able to change jobs without losing their accumulated pension rights.
In our increasingly technical society change comes rapidly. It is not enough that we provide trade and technical schools for the training and retraining of workers; we must also ensure that change of employment will not jeopardize the security of the workers. The labour force should not be penalized by the changing nature of industry which requires a great mobility of the working force. A man ought to be free to change from job to job, to change from trade to trade, to change from area to area without severely risking his future security.
A compulsory, national pension plan which is completely portable is a significant step in insuring greater mobility of the work force. Of course, we realize other measures will have to be adopted at various levels in order to give a greater mobility to the labour force. The supply of skilled labour will require greater flexibility than hitherto has been the case, and in this age of technological change, as new skills come into demand, there will have to be qualified men and women to fill the jobs that will be vacant. This mobility not only means mobility from one area to another but it also implies workers having to change their types of work as older skills become obsolete. A proper environment must be developed in which the working man will be able to cope with these changes and reap the benefits from technological change along with the rest of society.
The second major accomplishment of cooperative federalism which is prominent in this plan is the inclusion of supplementary pensions for widows, orphans and disabled

contributors. This is a field which, prior to the recent constitutional amendment, was enjoyed entirely by the provinces. The white paper points out that those under the age of 65 who will be eligible for supplementary pension will also draw a flat rate of $25 a month because these people will not, of course, be eligible for old age security. However, I think it is important to note that these supplementary pensions would be small if, in the early years of the plan, they were subject to the same ten year build-up as retirement pensions, and the government is to be commended on not including this ten years buildup as a provision applying to supplementary pensions. In a sense, therefore, supplementary benefit pensions are more generous, especially for those in the lower income brackets, than the new retirement pensions. This approach is justified because of the special need of widows, orphans and disabled contributors, and is certainly warranted on both humanitarian and economic grounds.
This plan at best can provide only minimum levels of retirement benefits. Because of the nature of their circumstances, widows, orphans and disabled contributors will not be in the same position to provide for themselves as well as able-bodied members of the work force can. These reasons justify the special way the government has approached this particular category. The approach is also justified because for the first time we will be making an attempt to have national standards in the case of widows, orphans and disabled contributors.
In the past great anomalies existed within the framework of our social security laws, and the greatest anomaly has been in this particular area because it is exclusively provincial and some provinces do not have the same resources as others to take care of orphans, widows and disabled contributors. This is particularly true of the Atlantic region, and therefore I think I can say the people of that region are very grateful the government has shown the wisdom of including these supplementary pensions. They are also grateful that this was able to be accomplished during the past year because, with the continuation of the existing approach undertaken by the respective provinces, this can lead to a more enlightened approach than has hitherto been undertaken with respect to this neglected group.
A number of members have commented on the inclusion of the self-employed in the plan. I would like to point out to them, and in particular to the hon. member for Perth who
Canada Pension Plan
seemed to be taking issue with this, that they are overlooking the fact that an abnormally high number of the self-employed are in the low income group. This is particularly true in the Atlantic provinces. For example, in Newfoundland some 20,000 people are employed in the fishing industry, the biggest single employer in the province, and the vast majority of them are self-employed. It is significant to note that, according to the white paper, the way the plan is to be administered will mean a more generous treatment of the low income group.
This is only as it ought to be because it is good economics. The people in the low income group have a greater struggle to meet the basic expenditures required to provide bare subsistence, and therefore they do not have great resources to provide for their retirement years.
There is another reason why it is a good thing to include self-employed people. There are so many of them in the lower income group, and I would hope this legislation will not be held out as the end-all and be-all of any administration's approach to the problems of the people in that group. I hope there will be a vigorous attempt made to create an environment in which these people, particularly those in the Atlantic provinces, can work to move into higher income groups. It would be a mistake to exclude them from this pension plan because we are hopeful that in the not too distant future the earned income of the average fisherman, logger and farmer in eastern Canada will be considerably higher than it is now.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre also dealt with the position of the people in the low income group. I did not completely understand what he said but I rather got the impression that he was ignoring the fact that there is something of a transfer of income in the present administration's approach to the inclusion of people in the low income group. This is a significant step forward to the realization of the goal of equal opportunities for all Canadians.
The benefits to be provided under this plan will be of great significance to all the people of Canada because the government of Canada is in fact providing a service which otherwise would not be provided. In the 1960's we talk about our great industrial progress, yet two thirds of our work force are without adequate pensions. It is obvious to all but the most narrow-minded nineteenth century thinker that this is the only way and the best way to go

Canada Pension Plan
about helping to provide security in old age. This is especially true in the case of those people who will benefit from the supplementary pensions because, as I mentioned earlier, this is a group which has been passed over in the past.
Though we talk about $75 a month being inadequate for people aged 70 years, this is a fortune compared with what is paid to some widows in parts of the country. If we have a sound philosophy on social security these anomalies can be ironed out, and I believe the introduction of this pension plan is the most significant step taken by any government in the realization of the need for such a philosophy.
As I said earlier, the one third we hear so much talk about, the one third who live on a bare subsistence level, cannot purchase for themselves through private insurance companies the pension plans that would provide them with some security in their old age. The benefits that they may be able to buy for themselves at present are not as great as we would like them to be, simply because of the fact that these people are in the low income group. I believe we cherish the hope, however, that after 30 years of acceptance of the government's role in the economy we shall reach a point where there will not be many people living at mere subsistance levels in this country. By including these people in the plan now, at a time when they do not have the resources to join private plans, we shall, as their incomes rise in the years ahead, have provided them with an opportunity to prepare for their years of retirement.
This pension plan is significant for many reasons, but the one I have tried to talk about is the mobility it will give to the Canadian labour force. It will not solve completely the problems caused by lack of mobility, but it is a step forward.
A second feature of the plan which appeals to me and to the people of Newfoundland is the inclusion of supplementary benefits. What this government has attempted to do in the Canada pension plan is consistent with what Abraham Lincoln had to say 100 years ago about the role of government:
The legitimate object of government is to do for a community of people whatever they need to have done but cannot do at all or cannot do so well for themselves in their separate and individual capacities.
I think this succinctly explains what the government is seeking to do in bringing forward this pension plan. I do congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare

on her achievement, one which must be all the sweeter in view of the bitterness which surrounds so many of the other things we do in this House of Commons.

There have been so many excellent contributions to the debate this afternoon that many of the points I wish to raise have already been covered, and covered well. There have been some references to the reasoned and reasonable statement made by the minister when she introduced this measure and made her initial statement in the house, and I am not at all surprised when I remember that within the last seven days she has visited the keystone province of Canada; the moderating atmosphere of Manitoba may have had something to do with the moderation of her statement this afternoon. She mentioned that there may be honest differences over various facets of the pension plan. I am glad she does recognize that there are different ways of looking at this question and different ways of viewing the needs of the people who will be involved. I am impressed by the gigantic scope of this scheme. When this plan was introduced initially, I believe the minister told us it was the most far-reaching legislation to have been placed before the house for many decades. This being so I feel we should be cautious and careful in our approach; we should seek to devise the kind of plan which is the best we can muster.
I am pleased to note that in the house today there has been no rancour, but rather an atmosphere of unity in recognizing the need for a Canada pension plan. The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska spoke of the ways in which this plan illustrated the new phrase "co-operative federalism" we hear so often. The very fact that this is an example of an area where a province could actually opt out, as the phrase is, yet still be part of a national plan is perhaps a particularly good illustration of co-operative federalism. The only feature I am worried about in this connection is standards. The speaker who preceded me said this was a grand national plan, and that it would be raising standards in all the provinces. However, if the other provinces choose to invoke the privilege of opting out of a national program, is there machinery in this plan which would ensure that there will still be the national standards at which we have aimed in devising this scheme?
In my general endorsation of this plan I wish to inject some words of caution. I do so, not for the sake of making carping criticism but because I think we need to look

very carefully at the effect this plan would have on our people and on our economy in general. I know that in Manitoba our premier, Mr. Duff Roblin, has spoken of the crisis of priorities. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent has already touched on this question of priorities. I feel justified in making further reference to it, however, because of the fact that the federal system under which this country operates makes it possible for both federal and provincial governments to impose taxes in the same tax areas. Personal income tax, for example, is a legitimate field for taxation by provincial governments as well as by the federal government and the same is true of corporation income taxes. In other areas, there is a separation-I refer to provincial sales taxes, for example, and on the other hand to excise taxes, which are purely a federal concern. But whatever the method of taxation used may be, the tax is always levied on the same resources-the only wealth generating power in the nation, namely the taxpayers.
It should be stated frankly that the combined taxation forces of the provincial governments and the federal government already take almost 25 per cent of the gross national product and I think common sense begs that we should look carefully at just where we are going. Are we getting the best value for our dollar? I share the anxiety of previous speakers over these expenditures. I think the Canada pension plan is a grand design. It is part of a further mosaic in our whole social security design. Earlier I spoke of the need for pulling together the various social security measures we already have and which have grown up piecemeal to deal with various areas of need, disability, old age, and so on. Here we have another piece added to the mosaic in the form of the Canada pension plan.
I am still hopeful that somehow we shall evolve a plan which will make one large social security parcel, whether we call it that or not, designed to meet the needs of people in all the various categories. The plan as introduced goes part of the way. It deals with benefits to survivors, to disabled people and to orphans and in this sense it is a great step forward, not just a piecemeal measure but an encompassing measure. It will certainly cost a great deal of money. If we are to demand revenue to meet this kind of expenditure from the public purse, I must say I share Premier Roblin's concern about priorities and I sometimes wonder whether we have placed the demand in the proper area. For
Canada Pension Plan
my part I feel that expenditure on our younger citizens pays by far the greatest dividend, and expenditure on the young must, naturally, be aimed at improving education. I know this is a field which is not within the federal sphere. But we are witnessing increasing examples of education being interfered with as a result of the mobility of our population. As they travel from one province to another families must adapt themselves to changes in educational programs. Families of members of parliament are among those who encounter this difficulty. All of us run up against this vast problem of different standards in education. I think if we devised some way of channeling the spiralling costs of education in proper perspective with other demands on public money, this would certainly serve us well in the apportioning of public expenditures, which we seem to have to do in every session.
A pension makes reference to the fact that there is an incentive to keep persons employed; that is, if you keep on working until you are 70 years of age, your pension benefits will be larger than if you choose to retire and take your pension at age 65. This is somewhat at variance with what automation does to the labour force, because surely all the indications are for earlier retirement and fewer opportunities for employment for the older individual. This is just one area of contradiction that I point out. I do not think this is necessarily a fault of the plan, but this will be one of the things we will have to fit into the scheme as automation takes its unending course, which course we cannot alter.
The fact that the lowest income group, those persons not earning $600 per year, is not covered may be an area of concern. I have no suggestion to offer as to how these people can be included; but we ask ourselves, is it fair to eliminate a group here, even if they wish to participate in benefiting from this plan? Perhaps it will still be possible to do this when we are considering the bill at the clause by clause stage; but it seems there will be a significant number of individuals who will not be able to become part of this scheme, even if they elect to do so.
There will be one very obvious defect which other hon. members have already pointed out. That is the fact that those persons who are at the present time 70 years of age will of course not be helped at all, and those persons of 55 years of age and over will not be able to benefit to the maximum degree from the scheme because of the diminishing returns

Canada Pension Plan
if they have not worked the full ten years. On the other hand there will be windfalls to those persons who began contributing exactly or approximately ten years before their retirement. This windfall will be in the nature of receiving benefits far in excess of the amounts they have contributed. For example, very roughly I suppose a person who retires ten years from the date the plan comes into effect will have contributed an average of perhaps $900 toward the plan, but he will benefit to the extent of $1,250 for every year he lives. So this is an obvious windfall to those persons who are in the fortunate age group of about 50 or 55 at the time this plan comes into effect.
It has already been pointed out that younger persons will have contributed for as long as 52 years and will still only receive the same benefits. These are difficulties which perhaps cannot be solved in the plan, so there will be greater equity; but none the less, rather than saying we must have something that will fit everyone, it just will not be possible to develop a general scheme to fit everyone, and perhaps we will have to accept the plan with these difficulties. I believe another area of greater concern will be the problem of integrating private plans. I am sure that many, many workers are worried about how this plan will affect their present superannuation plans or schemes. I can see no way in which iron-clad rules can be developed to fit the integration of the private plan in the Canada pension plan, and it seems to me to become a large problem of examining and adapting each private scheme to the Canada pension plan. This in itself will prove an added difficulty.
Mr. Chairman, I just wanted to make a brief reference to a comment the Porter royal commission on banking has made about the plan. Certainly this is a thoughtful study to which I am making reference. They make the comparison of the Canada pension plan, attempting to provide benefits far greater than the American social security measures even though our national per capita income is something like 30 per cent below the American per capita income. Mention is made of the fact that the average contribution will be something like 3 per cent, perhaps 3.6 per cent for those in the higher income groups and the self-employed. But we must not forget the fact that we are already paying 4 per cent on our old age security tax; so actually when we speak of drawing a pension of $179, it will be paid for by having levied on us a tax of not 3.6 per cent but generally 3 per cent, for
[Mr. Enns.l
a total tax of 7 per cent. This comes quite close to the current cost of the American plan, and it is threatening to go higher. I am just wondering, in view of the fact that we are hoping to benefit more than the American social security measure with paying 7 per cent, whether we will not also be faced with an increasing levy on this 3 per cent plus 4 per cent. These are just some of the reservations that come to mind about this scheme. Generally I must endorse it and say that it is a very welcome measure. I am, with other members, looking forward to seeing the details of the bill and to this end hope that before long it will be referred to the joint committee to which the minister has already made reference.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that a very great deal has been made of the fact that we are now entering into the No. 3 version of the Canada pension plan. The hon. member for Perth made reference to some previous, ill-fated efforts, it seemed to me in an attempt to show that this government had no clear idea what we were trying to achieve. Therefore I would like to review some of the events that led up to introduction of the present plan. The hon. member for Perth also mentioned action taken by the previous administration. I noticed he was very brief in his references to that previous action; as a matter of fact, he seemed to skip over it very hurriedly, and I can certainly understand that.
First, Mr. Chairman, while we realize this is a field of joint federal-provincial jurisdiction, no contributory, portable pension legislation had been proposed by any jurisdiction up to the general election of 1962 and 1963. While the Liberal party and the New Democratic party campaigned extensively on such a platform, no objections were heard at that time from any of the provincial governments. On July 18, 1963, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare outlined in this house what hon. members opposite like to refer to as the first version, we had had at that time the introduction of the Ontario pension plan, which in fact was a plan which regulated private plans in those companies that had 15 or more employees. No one has tried, seriously at least, to argue that the Ontario plan was a solution to the problem, and in fact I think one could say its objectives rather complement the objectives that the present Canada pension plan embodies.
What were the essential features of the July proposals of the minister? The plan was compulsory for employees. It was voluntary

for the self-employed. It provided for portability of pensions anywhere in Canada-as universal a coverage as was administratively possible. It provided for a relatively short maturity period of ten years in an attempt to make some provision for the middle aged and older workers. It provided for a level of benefits varying from between 20 to 30 per cent of earnings, dependant on the retirement age. If we consider the average retirement age at 67J, the benefits proposed were 25 per cent. These rose to 30 per cent at age 70. The maximum pension at age 70 was to be $100 a month plus the $75 flat rate old age security.
The contributions were to be applied to the national average of earnings and were initially to be 1 per cent from the employee and 1 per cent from the employer. These contributions were also to be used to finance the $10 increase in the old age security program. They were also designed to make the plan essentially a pay as you go scheme. We had further protection against inflation by relating benefits to the average level of earnings at the time of retirement. We also had some provision for retirement at age 65 although at a reduced level of benefits. This applied both to the flat rate and to the contributory schemes.
There was also some provision made for survivor benefits after age 65, and the minister at that time offered full co-operation to the provinces-in fact, invited the cooperation of the provinces-in extending this to widows and orphans allowances, as well as disability benefits under the plan.
We all recall, Mr. Chairman, the initial storm that these proposals raised, mainly amongst individuals in the insurance industry. A number of arguments were made to the effect that the plan was too generous, that there would be an interference with the capital formation of our economy, and so on. In addition to this, last September the government of Quebec announced that they were going to set up their own plan and would not participate in the federal scheme. Premier Robarts of Ontario also indicated that he was not too satisfied with the plan, but it seemed to me that his objections took a somewhat different tone. It was my own impression that his objections sounded remarkably like those which emanated from the insurance industry. Other provinces also raised a number of questions, but it became apparent that, with Quebec out, Ontario was essential to the plan. These two provinces represented two thirds of the
Canada Pension Plan
population in the country and their exclusion would mean violation of one of the fundamental principles of a contributory national portable plan.
Therefore, because of the provinces, and primarily because of Ontario, the pension plan was modified. In an attempt to meet the criticisms particularly of Ontario, the level of benefits was reduced to 20 per cent of earnings at age 70. This was to answer the charges of extravagance and to leave additional room for private plans. The second change was that although the contributions remained at 1 per cent plus 1 per cent, the income ceiling was raised to $4,500. This was frozen, however, for five years in an attempt to facilitate the integration of private plans. Because the $10 increase in old age security had been separated and was to be financed out of other revenues, partial funding was possible. An estimated $2.5 billion was anticipated in the initial ten year period, 50 per cent of which was to be invested in provincial securities. In spite of considerable pressure the maturity period was maintained at ten years, which was a very important feature of the plan.
This was the mark II version, if you will, which was introduced in March 1964, and which was to be the basis of discussion at the federal-provincial conference in April of this year. It was at that conference that the Quebec government revealed the outline of what became known as the Quebec plan. Hon. gentlemen opposite refer to somersaults and retreats. Certainly Premier Robarts of Ontario made in my opinion one of the most spectacular somersaults in recent times. After one look at the Quebec plan's benefits, and more particularly at the funding, he suddenly forgot his basic objection to our original plan and came out for a plan which was in many respects more generous than the original, that had a higher level of contributions and was therefore harder to integrate with existing schemes, and a plan which interfered far more with the flow of savings into private institutions, a fact which he had been very concerned about a few months previously.
I should like to quote from an article by Bruce Macdonald which appeared in the Globe and Mail of April 14 last concerning this change of attitude on the part of the Ontario government. He said:
For many months, Premier Robarts pressed to have the Canada pension plan scaled down to a more modest program. Primarily as a result of his adamant stand, the federal government agreed earlier this year to trim the size of benefits and to modify the rate at which the scheme would go into effect.

Mr. Chairman, in the few minutes left before the conclusion of this debate I should like to make one or two points. A great number of questions that have arisen in our minds have been covered by various hon. members of this committee during the past few hours, and I certainly do not intend to repeat them.
In this party we do feel that the Canada pension plan, and all the details of what is going to be the plan, to be presented to parliament after this resolution stage is passed, in many respects has moved a long way from the original intention; that of having what one may call a universal portable pension plan for Canadians. I note there is a lack of reference to the Canada pension plan as being a portable pension plan. About two years ago the great concern expressed in this house was in respect of pensions being portable, particularly as between industries. There seems now to be a completely new concept of what a Canada pension plan should be.
During those days there was great concern because of the movement of workers from one industry to another, and from one area
to another, because of automation and other factors. We are now discussing a Canada pension plan which really has nothing to do with portability from one job to another, and from one area to another.
Mr. Chairman, that being the situation, there are many questions which have arisen in the minds of hon. members which have yet to be answered. In spite of the fact the Minister of National Health and Welfare has been asked on a number of occasions whether or not the province of Ontario has agreed to participate, we are still not aware of the situation. We know that there have been indications that provision will be made for any province to opt out and set up individual plans. On October 22 I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare whether or not all the provinces with the exception of Quebec had indicated either to her or to the government that they were prepared to participate. She did not give a straightforward answer. She said that all the provinces were represented at the last meeting at which this matter was discussed and that there was no indication from any province of non-participation. I reminded the minister that that was not the question I had asked, and that I had asked her if any province had indicated it was not willing to participate-other than the province of Quebec, which we know is not going to participate. Again she hedged by saying a number of things; she did not answer the question that was asked.
I think we have now reached a stage, by the introduction of this resolution preceding the bill, when we as members of this House of Commons have a right to a forthright answer as to whether or not the province of Ontario is going to participate in this plan. The reason I say that is that the province of Quebec is, not participating, and if the province of Ontario decides not to participate the plan cannot be considered as being national in scope.
By and large I am in favour of having laws passed by the federal government applicable to all Canadians in all parts of Canada. We realize of course that the amendments which were sought to the British North America Act, so that a pension plan could be brought in, require endorsation by all provinces. One of the conditions of agreeing to seek that kind of an amendment was that the provinces would have the right to opt out, if they so chose. It seems to me if we are going to have the two most populous provinces, Ontario and Quebec, representing something in the neighbourhood of 12 million of the 19 million

Canada Pension Plan
people, not participating, this House of Commons is wasting its time in dealing with a so-called national pension plan. I say that because if that happens we will have approximately only one third of the population covered by the plan. Perhaps the federal government has been negotiating with the province of Ontario to find out what their position is going to be. Perhaps the federal government has been seeking an indication from them whether or not they are going to participate. In any event, now that we have reached the stage that the resolution has been introduced in this house I think we have a right to know.
There are a number of reasons why I say this. If the province of Ontario is not going to participate I suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that there will be other provinces in addition to Ontario and Quebec which will have very serious reservations about being included in this plan, rather than setting up their own. There is more than one reason for that. One is that we will have lost the national coverage feature. A second is that no answers have been given to the provinces as to how the Canada pension plan is going to be reconciled, for example, with the public service pension plans that some of the provinces are now operating. If there is to be no clearcut reconciliation between these public service plans and the so-called Canada pension plan, then certainly some of these other provinces might just as well set up their own pension plans because they will be in the business of operating and administering a pension plan anyway.
The undesirable feature of belonging to the so-called Canada pension plan and having to operate these other pension plans is that the provinces would then be subjected to the responsibility of administering a plan with regard to which the legislation and the regulations would be under the control of another body than their own legislatures. So it becomes very obvious that, unless there is a clear statement very soon that, first of all, Ontario is going to participate and, second, that there is going to be a reconciliation with some of these other plans that provincial governments are obliged to administer now, many of the desirable features are lost and some of the inherent complexities are perhaps too great for the effort required.
I am going to conclude my remarks now with the hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will rise in her place in the next few minutes, take the members of the committee into her confidence and tell

them whether or not the province of Ontario is going to participate, and also whether or not there is going to be a general plan with regulations attached to it so that it will be possible for these other public service pension plans to be reconciled with this plan, in order that the provinces will not be in the awkward position of having to operate their own pension plans and also having to do those things necessary to carry out a law enacted in another place.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Miss LaMarsh thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-136, to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, today during the question period when I directed a question to the Minister of Agriculture asking him to inform the house of the reason why returns to feed lot farmers for feeder cattle have been lower this year than since 1962, he gave me as an answer the prices for choice dry feed cattle instead of for feeder lot cattle, which was incorrect and not based on my question at all.
I take as my authority the information contained in the magazine, Canadian Cattlemen in its November, 1964 issue. In it there is a table headed "Estimated Returns from Feeding" which gives the comparison prices for the years 1960-61, 1961-62, 1962-63 and 1963-64. From the last column in this table for the year 1963-64 it is seen that the return to the farmer, after all expenses counted, was a loss of $14.08 per head. This is based on a 700 pound feeder steer which the farmer buys in the fall and on a 1,000 pound steer which he markets in the winter or spring.
