Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
In 1960-61 his profit was $28.63 at a time when the cost of the feeder steer was $196 and when he could sell it for $225. In 1962-63 the farmer lost 0.24 cents but in the previous year, 1961-62, his profit was $23.34.
When the Minister of Agriculture contradicts these tables presented by the Canadian Cattlemen magazine he either does not want to admit that farmers during the last two years, since he became Minister of Agriculture, have sustained severe losses in the cattle market-and this applies also to chickens and turkeys-or he is not familiar with what is going on in these markets. Perhaps he figures that the farmers cannot calculate for themselves when they sustain losses or when they make profits. He should pay more attention to what is going on in these markets and should help bring about a situation in which the farmer can make some profit out of his farming enterprise.
That is all I have to say at the present time, but I am sure it will not be long before I have something else to discuss with the Minister of Agriculture.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
I wonder sometimes where hon. members opposite get some of the information they try to peddle in here. The facts are available to anyone, even to members of the opposition who are really interested in facts and not partisan fancies.
Earlier today the hon. member claimed that feeder cattle have been selling for $14 per head lower than last year. I quoted him the actual market figures which showed that there was less than a cent a point difference between this year's prices and last year's prices. I do not want to suggest that everything is perfect in the beef business today:
I would like the hon. member to show me any business anywhere, where everything is perfect.
I have a few facts which indicate beyond any argument that our beef business, like virtually every other business in Canada lately, is enjoying one of the best years in a long time, certainly better than any year between 1957 and 1963. In the first half of 1964 our gross national product was 8 per cent higher than in the first half of 1963. The index of industrial production for the first seven months was 9 per cent higher. All of this has contributed to a 13 per cent reduction in unemployment during the first nine months of this year. Agriculture and the beef business have enjoyed the benefits of this unprecedented prosperity along with other sections of our national economy. It


now appears likely that Canadians will use over one and one quarter billion pounds of beef this year. This is about 9 per cent more than last year and 27 per cent more than during the six years from 1957 to 1962. We have achieved this in spite of obstacles which even the miracle men of the Diefenbaker administration would have had trouble overcoming.
This has been achieved despite the fact our cattle population was 4 per cent higher than in 1963; despite the fact our feeder cattle exports for the first nine months were only 20,000 head compared to 54,000 head during the same period in 1963, and despite the fact our imports of beef were almost double our exports. These are the facts, and I think it is dangerously close to being irresponsible to try to paint a picture of disaster for our beef producers when this is simply not the case. I can think of nothing that would bring trouble to our beef industry faster, in fact, than if our producers should take this kind of wild statement seriously. Fortunately they know better.
But I do not want to suggest that the government is not concerned about the beef industry today. We are well aware that because of the present large beef population in the United States our prices are once more being influenced by the price for Canadian beef on the American export market. Because of the health of our economy, for the first time in many years our beef prices earlier this year were higher than the American price. Our beef market has now returned more nearly to normal. Export prices once more are tending to determine the price on our domestic market.
I can assure hon. members that the government is very much aware of the situation and that it has every intention of taking steps to keep our beef industry in a healthy condition should the situation deteriorate. But a lot of loose talk is not going to help one bit.
Tell that to the marines, not to members of parliament.

speechtext:
I was
very interested in hearing the minister's prepared statement, particularly as he began by saying he wondered where we were getting "the sort of stuff we were peddling". I only have to remind him that a week ago or a little longer-as a matter of fact it was on October 27-I put on record a letter from a

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
beef producer in my constituency. This letter I think supports in no uncertain terms the point of view put forward by my hon. friend.
The minister made a very definite statement out west about what he intended to do about this. He said a lot about the new agriculture policy he intended to bring in. But today, in the question period, the only people he mentioned were the milk producers. Well, we know they are doing all right. But how many farmers can get milk contracts? Very few.
The minister says things are much better now than they were between 1957 and 1962. That seems strange. This is in the Toronto Star of October 30, 1964. The minister said:
I think the last Liberal government had forgotten the farmers during its declining years-
Then he said:
I'll even go further-I think that on the basis of its record with our farmers-
If I may paraphrase it, Mr. Speaker, he thought our policy was a very good policy. Those are the minister's own words. But that is not why I rose this evening. The minister referred to my hon. friend's statement as being vile; he used that very word. Let me quote from the d.b.s. figures published by its agricultural division, where it is stated that six out of nine provinces-and mostly eastern, of course-were all lower in income at the end of 1963; and I understand the situation has deteriorated this year. If that is an improvement, he is going to have to show me where the improvement is-and if I am peddling trash he had better get in touch with d.b.s. and make that statement to them.
I have been responsible for raising the question of turkeys in this house on many occasions. I had the turkey producers at my home this past week end, and they told me that if the minister and the government do not take some action by the middle of November, their market to make anything whatsoever this year is lost-that is in connection with the importation of turkeys from the United States-because, as the minister will know better than I, around the middle of this month the freezer stocks are put on the market for the year-end business that is apt to accrue to these turkey producers. I will read their statement into the record. The minister has these publications; there is no question about that. In their summing up the Canadian turkey federation had this to say to the minister:
Due to the hardship being experienced right now by many of our growers due to the unprofitable market, we strongly urge the implementation of some measure-
Anything; they will grasp at any straw:
-as above or within the scope of the government, to bring immediate market improvement during the balance of the fast approaching main marketing season of 1964.
Then the last sentence reads:
Otherwise, later help developed from the foregoing recommendations may be too late to save many of our growers.
They said the same thing in a previous petition to the government. Surely the minister is well aware of what the situation is, and we are not exaggerating it; we only want to bring to his attention that it is deteriorating and the income of the eastern farmers is declining. I went on to say in a previous statement-I do not know whether the minister was here-that ever since his party has been in office the income of the eastern producers has been going down, down, down. I said it at that time and I meant it. I have this letter here. I do not want to read it again, but there is no question about the situation; the income of this farmer is down in every phase of his operation. The figures are here and the minister can read them if he wants to do so. This is caused by the increase in price of the things the man has to buy, compared with the profit he makes, which is diminishing. He concludes by saying:
With prices like this and the high cost of labour, machinery, taxes (etc.), which you know as much about as I do, how in the world is the farmer going to exist?
This man is a very good, knowledgeable farmer; he belongs to all the organizations that can assist him-and he is complaining bitterly about the lack of government action to support the eastern producers. If the minister is not convinced he should go directly into the rural areas of eastern Canada and western Ontario, where my constituency in fact is, and they will tell him. If he does not know this, there is no sense talking to him any longer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-STEPS TO IMPROVE POSITION OF EASTERN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to start with I am a little tired of all the doom crying we keep hearing from the opposition about the plight of the eastern farmer. If the Tories are really as seriously concerned as they try to make out, why did they not do something for eastern farmers? After all, they had six years and the biggest majority in history. We have only had about 18 months to work on these problems, but in going through the record I find it would be impossible to do justice to
9934	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion what has already been achieved by the present government, in the limited time at my disposal.
In the dairy industry, for example, our policies have reduced the exorbitantly expensive surplus of butter to normal supply levels. The skim milk market has been stabilized and producers prices have been pushed to near record levels. We are having the highest production of cheese in eastern Canada that there has been in 15 years and more of this than ever before is quality cheese. We managed to get a 20 per cent increase in the American quota on Canadian cheese exports. As the president of the national dairy council, Mr. J. M. Hartwick, said recently, "The dairy industry is enjoying the strongest sales position in many years."
Yet while our dairy farmers' incomes have increased we have reduced the cost of the dairy stabilization program. For the first six months of this year returns to eastern farmers from dairy products were $10 million higher than for the first six months of last year. Here are the figures for the dairy products for the first six months in 1963 and in 1964:
	1963	1964
	$	$
	Million	Million
Prince Edward Island	1.6	2.2Nova Scotia	5.7	5.8New Brunswick	5.1	5.4Quebec	72.6	74.6Ontario	93.4	100.4
It is widely recognized that one of the big problems in eastern agriculture arises from the fact that many of our farms are too small to be economic. The government has recognized this pressing need for our eastern farmers to expand their operations by greatly increasing the credit facilities our farmers need for this expansion. We have doubled the amount available from the Farm Credit Corporation. We have doubled the amount available under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. And we have introduced a totally new form of farm credit under the Farm Machinery Syndicates Act, an unsubsidized program that makes it possible for farmers in every part of Canada to reduce their machinery costs by two thirds or more. It is the direct responsibility of provincial govern-

ments to provide farmers with crop insurance. But we have done everything we could by providing crop reinsurance, or disaster protection, for the provinces, to encourage provincial governments to provide this important income stabilizer for farmers in all parts of the country.
We have heard a lot from opposition benches about the need to do something about eastern feed grain. The previous government had six years and did nothing. But within three months of taking office the present government introduced a policy of supporting winter storage costs which has stabilized both the supply and the price of western feed grain used by eastern producers. I could go on but my time is running out.
What disturbs me most about the distortion and misrepresentation which we hear so often about our eastern agricultural problems is that this sort of approach can only make the problems of eastern farmers worse. This can only confuse eastern farmers and mislead them into thinking their problems are one thing when they are really something else. This may very well make the problems worse than they are by convincing the farmers that they are worse off than they are. Any suggestion that eastern farmers are at a disadvantage as compared to western farmers just does not hold water when you look at the facts. Farmers in Ontario and Quebec are from 1,500 to 2,500 miles closer to the main markets of Toronto and Montreal, which gives the eastern farmer a natural advantage. Farm machinery prices are lower in the east than the west. For example the freight rate on a ten-foot heavy duty cultivator from Brantford is something like $50 to Regina, $55 to Swift Current but only $18 to Montreal. I think discussion and criticism of government policies in this house can be very helpful in letting the people know what is going on. But it should be informed and factual discussion, not misleading partisan wrangling which can only confuse the people.

subtopic: COMMUNIQUE FOLLOWING OTTAWA MEETING ON PEACE KEEPING OPERATIONS

speechtext:
A meeting of military experts to consider the technical aspects of United Nations peace keeping operations took place in Ottawa from November 2-6 inclusive at the invitation of the government of Canada. Commodore R. W. Murdoch of Canada acted as chairman. Representatives from the following countries attended: Brazil, Colombia, Denmark, Finland, Ghana, India, Iran, Ireland, Italy, Liberia, Malaysia, Morocco, Netherlands, New Zealand, Nigeria, Norway, Pakistan, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Sweden, Tunisia, United Arab Republic. Major-General Indar Rikhye, military adviser to the secretary general of the United Nations, attended the meeting as an observer.
Three working groups were established. Group 1, under the chairmanship of General Kittani, Morocco, (vice chairman Major General Kaldager, Norway) studied the questions of composition, command, control and liaison, training and operational problems. Group 2, under the chairmanship of Major General Ankrah, Ghana, (vice chairman Colonel Amati, Italy) studied questions relating to
environmental operating information and logistic support. Group 3, under the chairmanship of Mr. B. C. Mishra, India, (vice chairman Mr. O. Bierring, Denmark), studied personnel administration, public relations, accounting procedures, and legal problems.
The chairmen of the working groups reported to the delegates on the work of their groups at the final plenary session, following which there was discussion of some of the points made in the reports.
The meeting did not attempt to reach formal conclusions on the items discussed. However, delegates hoped that the exchange of views, both written and oral, would contribute to the effectiveness of such national forces as might be made available to the United Nations in the future and had therefore served the general purpose of strengthening the capacity of participating nations to support the United Nations to engage in peace keeping operations.
The meeting expressed its gratitude to the government of Canada for its invaluable assistance in the operation of the meeting.
Tuesday, November 10, 1964
